conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks for coming. I just got discharged a couple days ago, but last night I ate a quarter of a sandwich and everything came back—severe pain, nausea, vomiting, fevers, chills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Where’s the pain located?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same as before—epigastric and right upper quadrant. It hasn’t changed in months. I couldn’t even walk to my clinic, so I went to the ER instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds really tough. Any pain meds since then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I got some relief at the other hospital, but nothing in the last few hours. It’s getting worse again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, we’ll get you some IV Dilaudid to help with that. You mentioned vomiting—have you kept anything down today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not even ice chips. I dry heaved earlier. I can usually keep pills down, but not today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll start with IV meds and fluids for now. You’re on Zofran at home—want us to give that IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. And I haven’t had a bowel movement in two days. I can’t take my stool softeners by mouth. Can I get a suppository tomorrow morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We can give a Dulcolax suppository in the morning. Let’s focus on getting your nausea and pain under control first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain med should be kicking in soon. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better, thank you. The sharpness is gone, but it’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We reviewed your imaging from earlier today. The CT scan shows no signs of pancreatitis or kidney stones. Your gallbladder looks normal too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not pancreatitis again? But the pain feels just like the flares I’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan doesn’t show active inflammation. But we know your chronic pain is real. It’s possible this is a flare of your chronic pancreatitis, even if it’s not showing up on imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve lost about 20 pounds since this all started. I’m worried I’m not getting enough nutrition. Should I be on TPN?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your albumin level—it’s normal at 3.8. That suggests your protein stores are okay for now. We don’t think TPN is needed, but we can connect you with a dietitian to talk about nutritional support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d really appreciate that. I’m trying to keep up with school, but missing classes is hard—even if I still have straight A’s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great managing all this. We’ll make sure you’re stable before discharge. Now, about your methotrexate—your PCP is continuing it weekly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 25 mg weekly. I was supposed to see my doctor today to talk about increasing the dose, but I missed the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We confirmed with their office. We’ll give you the methotrexate injection tonight. But the skin biopsy didn’t show vasculitis—so we’re not entirely sure what’s driving the inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it still helping? I feel like I need something to keep this under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may still be helping your malabsorption, which has improved. But we’re not seeing clear evidence of active vasculitis. Your PCP will help decide if the dose should go up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain and nausea today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I haven’t vomited since last night. I might be able to try some liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll start you on clear liquids—water, broth, apple juice. If you keep that down, we’ll advance to full liquids, then regular food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my constipation? I had the suppository this morning and had a bowel movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ll switch to oral Senna and add bisacodyl as needed. Avoid narcotics when possible—they make it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, but the pain is so bad sometimes I have to take the Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. We’re balancing pain control with side effects. Your POTS is stable—we’re continuing fludrocortisone and betaxolol as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another syncopal episode. I’m just frustrated—this keeps happening, and I don’t feel like anyone is coordinating my care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’ll make sure your PCP and specialists are updated. You’re seeing Dr. ___ soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not for a few weeks. I wish it were sooner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll flag that for your team. For now, focus on advancing your diet and staying hydrated. You’re making good progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well—tolerated full liquids, now moving to a regular diet. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I had a small meal and felt okay. Still some discomfort, but manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if this continues. No new medications—just your usual ones with a few adjustments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Adjustments? I thought I was going home on the same meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re lowering your escitalopram and betaxolol doses slightly—based on how you’re doing. You’ll take 10 mg escitalopram and 10 mg betaxolol daily. The rest stays the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s fine. And I’ll follow up with my doctors?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your PCP and specialists are aware. Try to keep those appointments—they’re important for managing your chronic conditions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made it through the night with no issues. We’ll discharge you in an hour or so. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one—should I worry about the weight loss? I still feel like I’m not eating enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your albumin is normal, which is reassuring. Keep working with your care team on nutrition. Maybe ask your PCP for a dietitian referral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you—for listening. It means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.
